summary: Proxy Mobile IPv6 lets a mobile node connect to one domain through several interfaces. This standards-track RFC adds extensions for network-based flow mobility across them, covering what the local mobility anchor and mobile access gateway do. It updates RFC 5213.

eli5.summary: A phone with Wi-Fi and cellular can have each conversation use a different one, moved around by the network.

questions: what is a local mobility anchor
what is a mobile access gateway
subtitle: How a Proxy Mobile IPv6 network can move individual traffic flows between a device's interfaces.

tldr.problem: A mobile node with several interfaces can attach to the same Proxy Mobile IPv6 domain through different access networks, but base PMIPv6 cannot move specific flows from one interface to another.
tldr.mechanism: The local mobility anchor manages which prefixes each interface gets, keeps a flow-level cache, and uses two messages, Flow Mobility Initiate and Acknowledgement, to tell the new gateway what to route.
tldr.outcome: Flows can be moved across interfaces by the network, using new Handoff Indicator, notification reason and status values. The RFC updates RFC 5213.

today: RFC 7864 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2016. It updates RFC 5213, and the metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Proxy Mobile IPv6 (PMIPv6, RFC 5213) gives hosts network-based mobility. It has two functional entities: the Local Mobility Anchor (LMA), which assigns one or more Home Network Prefixes (HNPs) to the mobile node (MN) and anchors all its traffic, and the Mobile Access Gateway (MAG), which detects the MN's attachment and provides IP connectivity.

PMIPv6 already lets an MN connect to one domain through different interfaces. This document adds extensions between the LMA and MAGs for flow mobility, which distributes specific traffic flows over different physical interfaces. Two things are required: proper prefix management by the network, and consistent flow forwarding policies.

The MN is assumed to attach to multiple MAGs, simultaneously or in sequence. Ways to achieve this include the logical interface of RFC 7847, or configuring the MN's IP stack for the weak host model of RFC 1122.
sections.eli5: A phone can be connected in two ways at once. This RFC teaches the network to decide which conversation goes through which connection.

sections.title: Use Cases and Who Decides
sections.content:
Unlike a typical handover, where one connection is dropped and another set up, flow mobility assumes the MN has simultaneous access to more than one network. The LMA is assumed to know this; how it learns that is out of scope.

There are two basic scenarios. In the first, a new attachment gets the same prefix or prefixes as an existing session. This is not base PMIPv6 behavior, so the LMA must be able to assign the same prefixes for a simultaneous attachment. In the second, a new attachment gets new prefixes, which is the default PMIPv6 behavior. A hybrid is also possible, where local policy decides whether a new prefix is exclusive to the new attachment.

Both the MN and the LMA MUST have local policies so packets are forwarded coherently in both directions. Either one can initiate flow mobility, but for a given MN the decision MUST be taken by the MN or by the LMA, and MUST NOT be taken by both.
sections.eli5: Sometimes both connections share one address, and sometimes each has its own. Either your phone or the network can decide to move a conversation, but never both at once.

sections.title: Moving Flows: Shared and Separate Prefixes
sections.content:
Shared prefixes. If the LMA gives the same prefix set to every interface, each MAG already knows how to route after its normal PBU/PBA registration, and moving a flow is just a local decision at the LMA. No extra signaling is needed, though it MAY be exchanged if a MAG needs flow-level information, for example to link flows with QoS paths. A new Handoff Indicator value, Attachment over a new interface sharing prefixes (6), lets the MAG tell the LMA that the same prefixes MUST be assigned. The RFC updates the binding cache rules of RFC 5213 section 5.4.1 so such a request either updates an existing entry or creates a new session sharing the same HNPs.

Different prefixes. If each interface has its own prefixes, the MAGs must be told about prefixes they do not anchor. Because an LMA cannot send a PBA that was not triggered by a PBU, this RFC uses two messages, FMI and FMA, in the format of the Update Notifications of RFC 7077. The LMA builds a Flow Mobility Initiate (FMI) with a Home Network Prefix Option for each prefix to support on the new MAG, with the off-link bit (L) set to one, and sends it to the new target MAG. The MAG MUST NOT advertise these prefixes on the MAG-MN link. The MAG replies with a Flow Mobility Acknowledgement (FMA).

When the trigger is a new interface attachment, the PBA answering the PBU can carry the same information as an FMI. The LMA then MUST include the Home Network Prefix Options with the L bit set to one.
sections.eli5: If both connections share an address, the network just changes its mind about the path. If they have different addresses, the network sends a short note to the new gateway saying, here come some extra addresses, please route them.

sections.title: Message Formats
sections.content:
The Home Network Prefix Option gets a new flag, L (off-link). When set, the MAG does not host the prefix on-link on the point-to-point interface with the MN, but treats it for flow mobility and adds it to its routing table. If L is 0, the MAG assumes the prefix is hosted on-link. The rest of the option is as in RFC 5213.

The FMI is the UPN message of RFC 7077, unchanged, with a new Notification Reason, FLOW-MOBILITY (8): a request to add or refresh the prefixes in the options in the set for which flow mobility is provided. Its Mobility Options field MUST hold the MN-ID followed by one or more Home Network Prefix Options. Prefixes previously enabled but absent from the message MUST be removed.

The FMA is the UPA message of RFC 7077, with new status codes: 0 (Success), 131 (Reason unspecified) and 132 (MN not attached). When the status is 0, its Mobility Options MUST contain the MN-ID followed by one or more Home Network Prefix Options.

Only the UPN and UPA messages with these values must be implemented; no other aspect of RFC 7077 is required.
sections.eli5: There is a new sticker on an address, meaning not here, just route it. The request and reply notes reuse an existing form with a few new answer boxes.

sections.title: Binding Cache and Flow Mobility Cache
sections.content:
The LMA's binding cache is extended to hold multiple Proxy-CoA registrations, as in RFC 5648: it keeps one entry per attached interface of an MN, each tied to a local Binding Identification (BID) number. An example in the RFC shows two entries for MN1, one over WiFi and one over 3GPP, sharing HNP1 but bound to two different MAGs.

Each LMA MUST also keep a Flow Mobility Cache (FMC), a conceptual list separate from the binding cache with one entry per registered flow. Each entry has a Flow Identifier Priority, a Flow Identifier, a Traffic Selector (TS), BIDs, an action (forward or drop) and an Active/Inactive state. Moving a flow means the LMA updates the BID the entry points to. An entry becomes Inactive only if all its BIDs are de-registered, and that does not affect data traffic.

A MAG MAY keep a similar structure. If it needs no full per-flow state its Binding Update List is enough; if it does need full per-flow state, it SHOULD also keep an FMC.
sections.eli5: The anchor keeps two notebooks. One lists which gateway each connection uses. The other lists each conversation and which connection it should take, so moving it means changing one line.

sections.title: Flow-Level Information and Mobile Node Duties
sections.content:
The RFC does not require flow-level information to be sent to the MAG; it only requires the LMA to keep it. If the MAG needs to know which flows are in a moved prefix, for QoS or to inform the MN, the LMA MUST include a Flow Identification Mobility Option for each such flow in the FMI or PBA, each with a Traffic Selector Sub-Option. To remove flow state, the LMA sends an FMI (or PBA) listing all flows to keep and simply omits the ones to remove. Even with a common set of prefixes, passing flow-level information needs this signaling.

The mobile node MUST be able to enforce uplink policies to select the right outgoing interface.
sections.eli5: Sometimes the gateway needs to know exactly which conversations are coming. The anchor sends a list, and anything left off the list is forgotten.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The new signaling shares the security concerns of Proxy Mobile IPv6 and, according to the RFC, poses no additional threats beyond those in RFC 5213 and RFC 7077. The MAG and LMA MUST use the IPsec mechanism mandated by Proxy Mobile IPv6 to secure this signaling.

IANA assigned: Handoff Indicator value 6 (Attachment over a new interface sharing prefixes), Update Notification Reason 8 (FLOW-MOBILITY), and Update Notification Acknowledgement Status values 131 (Reason unspecified) and 132 (MN not attached).
sections.eli5: The new notes are protected in the same way as the old ones. The new labels were registered in the official lists.
